claim: The cryo-electron microscopy structure of a PSI supercomplex incorporating fucoxanthin chlorophyll a/c-binding proteins (FCPs), designated as PSI-FCPI, was determined from the diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana CCMP1335.
source: In this study, we determined the cryo-electron microscopy structure of a PSI supercomplex incorporating fucoxanthin chlorophyll a/c-binding proteins (FCPs), designated as PSI-FCPI, isolated from the diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana CCMP1335.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental determination of the structure using cryo-EM.

claim: The PSI-FCPI structure from T. pseudonana reveals five FCPI subunits associated with a PSI monomer.
source: Structural analysis of PSI-FCPI revealed five FCPI subunits associated with a PSI monomer; these subunits were identified as RedCAP, Lhcr3, Lhcq10, Lhcf10, and Lhcq8.
evidence: The structure was determined experimentally and the subunits were identified.

claim: The five FCPI subunits in the PSI-FCPI structure are identified as RedCAP, Lhcr3, Lhcq10, Lhcf10, and Lhcq8.
source: Structural analysis of PSI-FCPI revealed five FCPI subunits associated with a PSI monomer; these subunits were identified as RedCAP, Lhcr3, Lhcq10, Lhcf10, and Lhcq8.
evidence: The subunits were identified through structural and sequence analyses.

claim: Specific protein–protein interactions were identified at the interfaces between FCPI and PSI subunits.
source: Through structural and sequence analyses, we identified specific protein–protein interactions at the interfaces between FCPI and PSI subunits, as well as among FCPI subunits themselves.
evidence: The interactions were identified through structural and sequence analyses.

claim: Specific protein–protein interactions were identified among FCPI subunits themselves.
source: Through structural and sequence analyses, we identified specific protein–protein interactions at the interfaces between FCPI and PSI subunits, as well as among FCPI subunits themselves.
evidence: The interactions were identified through structural and sequence analyses.

claim: Comparative structural analyses of PSI-FCPI supercomplexes, combined with phylogenetic analysis of FCPs from T. pseudonana and the diatom Chaetoceros gracilis, underscore the evolutionary conservation of protein motifs crucial for the selective binding of individual FCPI subunits.
source: Comparative structural analyses of PSI-FCPI supercomplexes, combined with phylogenetic analysis of FCPs from T. pseudonana and the diatom Chaetoceros gracilis, underscore the evolutionary conservation of protein motifs crucial for the selective binding of individual FCPI subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative structural and phylogenetic analyses performed in the study.

claim: Oxygenic photosynthesis in cyanobacteria, algae, and land plants converts solar energy into chemical energy and releases molecular oxygen into the atmosphere.
source: Oxygenic photosynthesis in cyanobacteria, algae, and land plants converts solar energy into chemical energy and releases molecular oxygen into the atmosphere (Blankenship, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established scientific literature.

claim: The conversion of light energy takes place within two multi-subunit membrane protein complexes, known as photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII).
source: The conversion of light energy takes place within two multi-subunit membrane protein complexes, known as photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII), which perform light harvesting, charge separation, and electron transfer reactions (Golbeck, 1992; Brettel and Leibl, 2001; Shen, 2015; Shevela et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established scientific literature.

claim: PSI and PSII perform light harvesting, charge separation, and electron transfer reactions.
source: The conversion of light energy takes place within two multi-subunit membrane protein complexes, known as photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII), which perform light harvesting, charge separation, and electron transfer reactions (Golbeck, 1992; Brettel and Leibl, 2001; Shen, 2015; Shevela et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established scientific literature.

claim: Numerous light-harvesting antenna subunits are associated with the periphery of the PSI and PSII core complexes.
source: To optimize light energy capture, numerous light-harvesting antenna subunits are associated with the periphery of the PSI and PSII core complexes, transferring excitation energy to the respective photosystem cores (Blankenship, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established scientific literature.

claim: Light-harvesting antenna subunits transfer excitation energy to the respective photosystem cores.
source: To optimize light energy capture, numerous light-harvesting antenna subunits are associated with the periphery of the PSI and PSII core complexes, transferring excitation energy to the respective photosystem cores (Blankenship, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established scientific literature.

claim: Light-harvesting antennae exhibit significant diversity among photosynthetic organisms, both in protein sequences and pigment compositions.
source: These light-harvesting antennae exhibit significant diversity among photosynthetic organisms, both in protein sequences and pigment compositions, and can be broadly categorized into two major groups: membrane proteins and water-soluble proteins (Blankenship, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established scientific literature.

claim: Light-harvesting antennae can be broadly categorized into two major groups: membrane proteins and water-soluble proteins.
source: These light-harvesting antennae exhibit significant diversity among photosynthetic organisms, both in protein sequences and pigment compositions, and can be broadly categorized into two major groups: membrane proteins and water-soluble proteins (Blankenship, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established scientific literature.

claim: The membrane protein category primarily consists of the light-harvesting complex (LHC) protein superfamily.

evidence: This is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: The red lineage encompasses red algae, diatoms, haptophytes, cryptophytes, and dinoflagellates.

claim: LHCs specific to PSI (LHCIs) bind to a eukaryotic PSI monomer, forming a PSI-LHCI supercomplex.

evidence: This is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: The structures of PSI-LHCI supercomplexes have been revealed by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) in various eukaryotes.

evidence: This is supported by citations to established scientific literature.

claim: In the red lineage, the number of LHCIs and their protein sequences and pigment compositions exhibit considerable variation among the PSI-LHCI structures of red algae, a diatom, a cryptophyte, and dinoflagellates.
source: In the red lineage, the number of LHCIs and their protein sequences and pigment compositions exhibit considerable variation among the PSI-LHCI structures of red algae (Pi et al., 2018; Antoshvili et al., 2019; You et al., 2023; Kato et al., 2024), a diatom (Nagao et al., 2020a; Xu et al., 2020), a cryptophyte (Zhao et al., 2023), and dinoflagellates (Li et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024).

claim: LHCIs have similar overall protein structures across photosynthetic organisms, with particular similarity in their three-transmembrane helices, regardless of whether they belong to the green or red lineages.
source: It is known that LHCIs have similar overall protein structures across photosynthetic organisms, with particular similarity in their three-transmembrane helices, regardless of whether they belong to the green or red lineages (Hippler and Nelson, 2021; Shen, 2022).

claim: Individual LHCIs have altered their sequences and structures to adapt their respective binding sites to the PSI cores during the assembly of PSI-LHCI supercomplexes.

claim: Diatoms are among the most essential phytoplankton in aquatic environments.

claim: Diatoms play a crucial role in the global carbon cycle, supporting marine food webs, and contributing significantly to nutrient cycling.
source: Diatoms are among the most essential phytoplankton in aquatic environments, playing a crucial role in the global carbon cycle, supporting marine food webs, and contributing significantly to nutrient cycling, thus ensuring the health and sustainability of marine ecosystems (Field et al., 1998).

source: Kumazawa et al. showed significant diversity in FCPs between C. gracilis and Thalassiosira pseudonana, with 46 and 44 FCPs identified, respectively (Kumazawa et al., 2022).

claim: FCPs are categorized into multiple, closely related subgroups.

source: However, an overall structure of the T. pseudonana PSI-FCPI supercomplex has yet to be solved.

claim: The structure of the PSI-FCPI supercomplex from T. pseudonana CCMP1335 was solved at a resolution of 2.30 Å by cryo-EM single-particle analysis.
source: In this study, we solved the structure of the PSI-FCPI supercomplex from T. pseudonana CCMP1335 at a resolution of 2.30 Å by cryo-EM single-particle analysis.
evidence: The structure was determined experimentally using cryo-EM.

claim: The PSI-FCPI structure reveals a PSI-monomer core and five FCPI subunits.
source: The structure reveals a PSI-monomer core and five FCPI subunits.
evidence: The structure was determined experimentally using cryo-EM.

claim: The final cryo-EM map was determined at a resolution of 2.30 Å with a C1 symmetry.
source: The final cryo-EM map was determined at a resolution of 2.30 Å with a C1 symmetry (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3, and Table 1), based on the 'gold standard' Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143 criterion (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The resolution was determined using standard cryo-EM data processing methods.

claim: The atomic model of PSI-FCPI was built based on the cryo-EM map obtained.
source: The atomic model of PSI-FCPI was built based on the cryo-EM map obtained (see Methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Tables 1–3).
evidence: The model was built using standard structural biology methods.

claim: The five FCPI subunits were named FCPI-1–5.
source: The five FCPI subunits were named FCPI-1–5 (Figure 1A), following the nomenclature of LHCI subunits in the PSI-LHCI structure of Cyanidium caldarium RK-1 (NIES-2137) (Kato et al., 2024).
evidence: The nomenclature follows a previous study.

claim: The positions of FCPI-1 and FCPI-2 in the T. pseudonana PSI-FCPI structure correspond to those of LHCI-1 and LHCI-2 in the C. caldarium PSI-LHCI structure.
source: Specifically, the positions of FCPI-1 and FCPI-2 in the T. pseudonana PSI-FCPI structure (Figure 1A) correspond to those of LHCI-1 and LHCI-2 in the C. caldarium PSI-LHCI structure.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The PSI core comprises 94 Chls a, 18 β-carotenes (BCRs), 1 zeaxanthin (ZXT), 3 [4Fe-4S] clusters, 2 phylloquinones, and 6 lipid molecules.
source: The PSI core comprises 94 Chls a, 18 β-carotenes (BCRs), 1 zeaxanthin (ZXT), 3 [4Fe-4S] clusters, 2 phylloquinones, and 6 lipid molecules, whereas the 5 FCPI subunits include 45 Chls a, 7 Chls c, 2 BCRs, 15 fucoxanthins (Fxs), 7 diadinoxanthins (Ddxs), and 3 lipid molecules (Table 3).
evidence: The cofactors were identified from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The 5 FCPI subunits include 45 Chls a, 7 Chls c, 2 BCRs, 15 fucoxanthins (Fxs), 7 diadinoxanthins (Ddxs), and 3 lipid molecules.
source: The PSI core comprises 94 Chls a, 18 β-carotenes (BCRs), 1 zeaxanthin (ZXT), 3 [4Fe-4S] clusters, 2 phylloquinones, and 6 lipid molecules, whereas the 5 FCPI subunits include 45 Chls a, 7 Chls c, 2 BCRs, 15 fucoxanthins (Fxs), 7 diadinoxanthins (Ddxs), and 3 lipid molecules (Table 3).

source: This unidentified subunit, designated as Unknown, occupies the same site as Psa28 in the C. gracilis PSI-FCPI (Nagao et al., 2020a).

claim: The structural comparison reveals that Unknown closely resembles Psa28 in the C. gracilis PSI-FCPI.
source: The structural comparison reveals that Unknown closely resembles Psa28 in the C. gracilis PSI-FCPI (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

source: However, Xu et al. referred to this subunit as PsaR in the PSI-FCPI structure of C. gracilis (Xu et al., 2020).

claim: Psa29 exhibits a unique structure distinct from the other PSI subunits in the T. pseudonana PSI-FCPI.

claim: Psa29 engages in multiple interactions with PsaB, PsaC, PsaD, and PsaL at distances of 2.5–3.2 Å.

claim: Sequence analyses suggest that Psa29 has undergone evolutionary divergence between Bacillariophyceae (diatoms) and Bolidophyceae.
source: Sequence analyses suggest that Psa29 has undergone evolutionary divergence between Bacillariophyceae (diatoms) and Bolidophyceae, the latter of which is a sister group of diatoms within Stramenopiles (Figure 2H), although this subunit has not been found in other organisms.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Bolidophyceae is a sister group of diatoms within Stramenopiles.
source: Sequence analyses suggest that Psa29 has undergone evolutionary divergence between Bacillariophyceae (diatoms) and Bolidophyceae, the latter of which is a sister group of diatoms within Stramenopiles (Figure 2H), although this subunit has not been found in other organisms.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge.

claim: Psa29 has not been found in organisms other than diatoms and Bolidophyceae.
source: Sequence analyses suggest that Psa29 has undergone evolutionary divergence between Bacillariophyceae (diatoms) and Bolidophyceae, the latter of which is a sister group of diatoms within Stramenopiles (Figure 2H), although this subunit has not been found in other organisms.

claim: Psa29 does not contribute to electron transfer reactions within PSI.

source: Each FCPI subunit binds several Chl and Car molecules: 7 Chls a/1 Chl c/2 Fxs/3 Ddxs/2 BCRs in FCPI-1; 10 Chls a/1 Chl c/3 Fxs/1 Ddx in FCPI-2; 7 Chls a/3 Chls c/2 Fxs/2 Ddxs in FCPI-3; 11 Chls a/2 Chls c/4 Fxs in FCPI-4; and 10 Chls a/4 Fxs/1 Ddx in FCPI-5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–E and Table 3).
